snip.t: | Aplastic anaemia | Pancytopenia, low retic, hypocellular marrow, no splenomegaly, possible exposure to benzene or radiation. | Bone‑marrow biopsy shows empty marrow; distinguishes from peripheral destruction. |
Under-production: iron, folate or B12 deficiency, HIV, TB, chronic kidney disease, malignancy, aplastic anaemia.
| Severe aplastic anaemia | Pancytopenia, no blasts, hypocellular marrow | Normal peripheral smear aside from low counts, absent clonal markers |
Decreased production: HIV, TB (marrow infiltration), malaria, sickle cell disease, aplastic anaemia, chemotherapy, severe malnutrition
Past haematological disease (sickle cell, thalassaemia, aplastic anaemia): Underlying marrow pathology predisposes to low platelets and may affect choice of definitive therapy.

qs.q: Which of the following describes the fundamental underlying defect in all cases of aplastic anaemia?
o: Increased peripheral destruction of mature circulating blood cells
Severe systemic iron deficiency impairing haemoglobin synthesis
Substantial reduction in haemopoietic pluripotential stem cells
Primary neoplastic infiltration of the bone marrow cavity by blasts
qs.e: The underlying defect in all cases of aplastic anaemia is a substantial reduction in haemopoietic pluripotential stem cells along with a fault in the remaining stem cells. Increased peripheral destruction leads to pancytopenia through a different path rather than primary bone marrow aplasia.
qs.s: Aplastic Anemia: Causes, Symptoms & Treatment Haematology: MCQs

qs.q: What is the characteristic physical examination finding regarding the liver, spleen, and lymph nodes in a patient with classic acquired aplastic anaemia?
o: Marked massive splenomegaly is commonly present
Lymph nodes, liver, and spleen are not enlarged
Hepatomegaly develops secondary to iron overload
Generalized painful lymphadenopathy is frequently found
qs.e: A key clinical feature of aplastic anaemia is that the lymph nodes, liver, and spleen are not enlarged. Hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy points towards alternative diagnoses like leukemia or infiltration.
qs.s: Aplastic Anemia: Causes, Symptoms & Treatment Haematology: MCQs

qs.q: Which immunological mechanism is predominantly implicated in the pathogenesis of idiopathic acquired aplastic anaemia?
o: Excessive stimulation of regulatory T cells suppressing erythropoietin production
Oligoclonal expansion of cytotoxic CD8+ T cells targeting haemopoietic tissue
Autoantibody production directed against mature circulating peripheral neutrophils
Complement-mediated lysis of pluripotential stem cells via CD55 deficiency
qs.e: Idiopathic acquired aplastic anaemia is driven by an autoimmune process dominated by the oligoclonal expansion of cytotoxic CD8+ T cells targeting haemopoietic tissue. Favourable responses to immunosuppressive agents like ATG and ciclosporin support this concept.
qs.s: Aplastic Anemia: Causes, Symptoms & Treatment Haematology: MCQs

qs.q: To establish the diagnosis of aplastic anaemia, bone marrow trephine biopsy findings typically demonstrate which of the following cellular changes?
o: Normal cellularity with selective maturation arrest of the erythroid lineage
Hypercellular marrow packed uniformly with immature blast cell forms
Hypoplasia with haemopoietic tissue replaced by fat comprising over 75%
Complete replacement of haemopoietic tissue by fibrosis and collagen
qs.e: Aplastic anaemia bone marrow shows hypoplasia where haemopoietic tissue is replaced by fat exceeding 75% of the marrow volume. Fibrosis is characteristic of myelofibrosis rather than aplastic anaemia.
qs.s: Aplastic Anemia: Causes, Symptoms & Treatment Haematology: MCQs

qs.q: Which of the following specific diagnostic exclusions must be performed in a patient presenting with acquired pancytopenia suspected to be aplastic anaemia?
o: Exclusion of hereditary spherocytosis via fragility
Exclusion of autoimmune anaemia using direct tests
Exclusion of G6PD deficiency using enzyme assays
Exclusion of Paroxysmal Nocturnal Haemoglobinuria
qs.e: Aplastic anaemia must be distinguished from other causes of pancytopenia, specifically requiring the exclusion of PNH by flow cytometry testing for CD55 and CD59. Osmotic fragility tests assess hereditary spherocytosis rather than pancytopenia.
qs.s: Aplastic Anemia: Causes, Symptoms & Treatment Haematology: MCQs

qs.q: Why must all blood products given as supportive care to patients with aplastic anaemia be leucodepleted?
o: To accelerate the recovery of endogenous neutrophil production
To completely eliminate the risk of bacterial transmission from donors
To reduce the viscosity of transfused packed red blood cells
To prevent alloimmunisation and avoid grafting of live donor lymphocytes
qs.e: Leucodepletion of all blood products is critical to prevent alloimmunisation and avoid the grafting of live donor lymphocytes which can cause transfusion-associated GVHD. It does not eliminate all bacterial risks or substitute for antibiotic therapy.
qs.s: Aplastic Anemia: Causes, Symptoms & Treatment Haematology: MCQs

qs.q: In the management of severe acquired aplastic anaemia, what is the preferred first-line specific treatment for a patient under 35 years of age who has an HLA-matching sibling donor?
o: Long-term maintenance therapy using recombinant human G-CSF alone
Repeated therapeutic phlebotomy combined with oral iron chelation therapy
Allogeneic stem cell transplantation offering a chance of permanent cure
High-dose systemic corticosteroid monotherapy administered over six months
qs.e: Allogeneic stem cell transplantation offers a chance of permanent cure and is favoured in patients under 35 years with severe aplastic anaemia who have an HLA-matching sibling donor. Immunosuppression is typically reserved for older or less suitable transplant candidates.
qs.s: Aplastic Anemia: Causes, Symptoms & Treatment Haematology: MCQs

qs.q: Which laboratory parameter threshold defines severe aplastic anaemia in terms of peripheral blood neutrophil count?
o: Less than 1.5 into ten to the power of nine per litre
Less than 0.1 into ten to the power of nine per litre
Less than 0.5 into ten to the power of nine per litre
Less than 1.0 into ten to the power of nine per litre
qs.e: Severe aplastic anaemia is defined by neutrophils <0.5 × 10⁹/L alongside platelets <20 × 10⁹/L, reticulocytes <20 × 10⁹/L, and marrow cellularity <25%. A neutrophil count below 1.5 × 10⁹/L represents the general diagnostic cutoff rather than the severe category criterion.
qs.s: Aplastic Anemia: Causes, Symptoms & Treatment Haematology: MCQs

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Aplastic anaemia is a life‑threatening marrow failure syndrome with pancytopenia and a markedly hypocellular, fatty bone marrow. It is usually immune‑mediated but can be secondary to infections, drugs, or toxins.

sections.p: Aplastic anaemia is defined by peripheral pancytopenia (Hb <10 g/dL, ANC <1.5 ×10⁹/L, platelets <150 ×10⁹/L) and a bone‑marrow biopsy showing <25 % cellularity with fatty infiltration.
b: Diagnosis requires exclusion of other causes of pancytopenia (e.g., megaloblastic anaemia, leukemia).
A normal or elevated serum erythropoietin supports marrow failure.

t.b: Does the patient have pancytopenia? Low values across all three lineages confirm marrow failure.
Is the marrow producing new red cells? Low retic (<1 %) indicates under‑production.
What is marrow cellularity? <10 % cellularity with fat confirms aplastic anaemia.
Is there a compensatory rise? Elevated EPO suggests marrow, not peripheral loss.
Is a secondary infection present? Positive results point to secondary aplasia.

sections.p: Severity is graded by absolute neutrophil count (ANC) and platelet count, using the Camitta criteria.
b: Severe: ANC <0.5 ×10⁹/L or platelet <20 ×10⁹/L.
Very severe: ANC <0.2 ×10⁹/L.

sections.p: Most cases are idiopathic (immune‑mediated). When a cause is identified, infections common in low‑resource settings are frequent.
b: Idiopathic (autoimmune T‑cell attack).
Viral: HIV, hepatitis B/C, parvovirus B19.
Bacterial/ TB: disseminated tuberculosis.
Drugs/toxins: chloramphenicol, benzene, herbal remedies.
Radiation or chemotherapy exposure.

sections.p: Patients develop symptoms of anaemia, infection, and bleeding due to loss of red cells, neutrophils, and platelets.
b: Fatigue, dyspnoea, pallor.
Fever, sore throat, recurrent infections.
Petechiae, bruising, mucosal bleeding.

sections.p: Beyond the core tests, additional studies help rule out mimics and assess organ involvement.
b: Serum ferritin to exclude iron overload from transfusions.
Flow cytometry if leukemia is suspected.

t.b: Is iron overload present? High ferritin may indicate transfusion‑related siderosis.
Is there clonal disease? Abnormal blasts suggest leukemia rather than aplasia.

sections.p: Rapidly falling neutrophils or severe bleeding can be fatal without urgent care.
b: ANC <0.2 ×10⁹/L → high risk of sepsis.
Platelets <10 ×10⁹/L → intracranial or gastrointestinal hemorrhage.
Progressive liver dysfunction from transfusion iron overload.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, provide supportive care, and consider definitive therapy (immunosuppression or stem‑cell transplant).
b: Remove offending drugs or treat infections first.
Immunosuppressive therapy: antithymocyte globulin + cyclosporine (targets autoimmune T‑cells).
Allogeneic hematopoietic stem‑cell transplant for young patients with HLA‑matched donor.
Supportive: transfuse packed RBCs for symptomatic anaemia, platelets for bleeding, and prophylactic antibiotics/antifungals for neutropenia.

sections.p: Regular monitoring of blood counts, iron status, and transplant eligibility is essential.
b: CBC every 2–4 weeks until stable, then monthly.
Serum ferritin every 3 months; start iron chelation if >1000 µg/L.
Vaccinate against encapsulated organisms before immunosuppression.

sections.p: Conditions that also cause pancytopenia must be distinguished.
b: Myelodysplastic syndromes – usually dysplastic cells on marrow, older age.
Acute leukemia – blasts >20 % on marrow.
Hypoplastic myelofibrosis – fibrosis on biopsy.
Nutritional anaemias – macrocytosis, low B12/folate.

sections.p: Certain labs may appear normal early or be altered by treatment.
b: Reticulocyte count can be falsely low after recent transfusion.
Serum EPO may be normal in early disease, rising later.
Peripheral smear may look normal despite severe marrow failure.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe dyspnoea or chest pain suggesting anemia‑related cardiac strain

faq.q: Why is EPO elevated in aplastic anaemia?
faq.a: The kidneys sense low oxygen from anaemia and increase EPO, but the marrow cannot respond because stem cells are destroyed.

faq.q: Can aplastic anaemia resolve without transplant?
faq.a: Yes, about one‑third of patients respond to immunosuppressive therapy and achieve transfusion‑independent remission.
It is essential to confirm hypocellularity and exclude leukemia or myelodysplasia.

exam: Describe the diagnostic criteria for aplastic anaemia and how you would differentiate it from myelodysplastic syndrome.
Explain the Camitta severity grading and its impact on treatment decisions.
Outline the first‑line immunosuppressive regimen and when stem‑cell transplantation is preferred.
